content.subtitle: Scripts for the lazy, the tinkerers, and the lazy tinkerers

paragraphs.name: 139e
paragraphs.text: Semi-automated migration from Bitbucket to GitHub: 2020 edition
Scripts for the lazy, the tinkerers, and the lazy tinkerers

paragraphs.name: 5e1a
paragraphs.text: In April, GitHub released new pricing plans that looked awfully affordable… and by affordable, we really mean free, because we don’t yet need the features on the new paid plans. As Bitbucket users since 2013, we have long been envious of the larger selection of integrations available to GitHub users. So with the new plans, coupled with cost-cutting pressure from COVID-19, this seemed like a great time to switch.

paragraphs.name: 0caf
paragraphs.text: We chose Bitbucket early on because their plans allowed for unlimited repositories. As programmers who didn’t like cleaning up our messes, you can imagine, we have collected many repositories over the last 8 years—175, to be exact. Far too many to move by hand! Encouraged by a helpful 2018 post and script from Continuum titled “Moving all your Bitbucket Repositories to GitHub”, we figured that wouldn’t be a blocker.

paragraphs.name: b6fc
paragraphs.text: Unfortunately, in the two years that passed, Bitbucket has since deprecated their version 1.0 API and we had to tweak things more than a little. And while modifying the code, we figured we would take the chance to tidy up our repositories by splitting them into different organisations, renaming them, providing better descriptions, and even archiving some of them right after migration. After finishing all this, we thought we should share this for anyone considering a similar move!

paragraphs.name: 22bc
paragraphs.text: So here’s our process for migrating all our repositories from Bitbucket to GitHub in 2020. We assume you already have your SSH keys set up for your Bitbucket and GitHub accounts.

paragraphs.name: af5a
paragraphs.text: Step 1: Extract a CSV list of all your Bitbucket repositories

paragraphs.name: ebef
paragraphs.text: Download the bash script list-bitbucket-repositories.sh from https://github.com/tinkertanker/bitbucket-github-migration:
From https://github.com/tinkertanker/bitbucket-github-migration

paragraphs.name: 2dd5
paragraphs.text: … then run it, fill in your username and password (perfectly safe, it just goes to Bitbucket—take a look at the source code, and at our footnote at the end of this article), and save the output to a CSV file, say bb_repositories.csv. You can choose any other name for the output file, of course.

paragraphs.name: abb9
paragraphs.text: $ bash list-bitbucket-repositories.sh > bb_repositories.csv

paragraphs.name: c24a
paragraphs.text: This gives you a CSV list of all the repositories you have access to, regardless of organisation. Open this up in your favourite spreadsheet app and you should get something like this:

paragraphs.name: 0f95
paragraphs.text: Step 2: Add headers and columns to prepare for migration, and take this chance to tidy up your repositories

paragraphs.name: da70
paragraphs.text: Add headers to the CSV that got generated in the previous step [BB Repo Name, BB Org, Description, Private]

paragraphs.name: 81e9
paragraphs.text: Add some columns so specify where in GitHub to send your repositories to, as well as whether to archive your repository after uploading. The final CSV field order should be [BB Repo, BB Org, GH Repo, GH Org, Description, Private, Archive]

Share this list with your teammates and take this chance to reorganise stuff and mark old repositories for archival. GitHub doesn’t have the same concept of Projects that Bitbucket does for organising repositories, but you can at least filter repositories on your dashboard by with the search query archived:false. Remove rows for repositories you don’t want to migrate too, of course.

paragraphs.name: 977b
paragraphs.text: Note: Don’t put any commas in any of the fields, not even the descriptions, or the script in Step 3 will get confused.
Here’s what your CSV should look like when you’re ready:

paragraphs.name: cbdd
paragraphs.text: Export or download your spreadsheet as a CSV file.
Step 3: Actually migrate your repositories

paragraphs.name: cb19
paragraphs.text: Download the bash script migrate-repositories-to-github.sh from https://github.com/tinkertanker/bitbucket-github-migration:

paragraphs.name: 2c9a
paragraphs.text: From https://github.com/tinkertanker/bitbucket-github-migration

paragraphs.name: 0f19
paragraphs.text: … then run it with your CSV file, say repository_mapping.csv, from Step 2 as the argument:

paragraphs.name: 621f
paragraphs.text: $ bash migrate-repositories-to-github.sh repository_mapping.csv

paragraphs.name: f41c
paragraphs.text: And it’ll go chugging along. Watch out for some possible errors:

paragraphs.name: 143b
paragraphs.text: Did you remember to remove all commas from your CSV? This method of parsing CSV really doesn’t do well with commas. If you see "message": "Problems parsing JSON" somewhere in your output, you probably left a comma in one of your descriptions.

paragraphs.name: 9a95
paragraphs.text: If you had any files larger than >100MB in your Bitbucket respository, you’ll see remote: error: GH001: Large files detected—these repositories will have to be moved manually. We haven’t figured out the best way to remove the large files without rewriting git history yet.

paragraphs.name: f45f
paragraphs.text: Don’t forget to check the repositories that were created in GitHub and see that they match and are not empty. Empty repositories won’t have a language detected. You can use search queries to filter repositories in GitHub, e.g. the querycreated:>2020-05-29T15:00:00+08:00would show only repositories created after 3pm on 29 May 2020, in timezone UTC+8.

paragraphs.name: d15d
paragraphs.text: And you’re done! If you have any suggestions or fixes, please send us an issue or pull request over at the GitHub repo. Happy migrating!

paragraphs.name: 411a
paragraphs.text: For migrating issues (as in, migrating the issues that were raised on your repo, not issues about migrating), we’re happy to report that this handy script still works and appears to be actively maintained (but of course, all migrated issues will be “opened” by the user doing the migration): https://github.com/jeffwidman/bitbucket-issue-migration

paragraphs.name: f0f5
paragraphs.text: Script implementation notes for the bash-curious!

paragraphs.name: da5f
paragraphs.text: For both scripts, we use read -p to prompt for usernames and passwords. The alternate approach of providing credentials on the command line, whether as an argument or by setting an environment variable, leaks your passwords to your bash history.
tail -n +2, in Line 2 of the migrate script, skips the header row from the CSV file.

paragraphs.name: be94
paragraphs.text: tr -d '\r', also in Line 2 of the migrate script, converts the line endings from DOS/Windows to Unix (and does nothing if the file is already using Unix line endings) — Google Sheets saves CSV files with DOS line endings.

paragraphs.name: 2fd0
paragraphs.text: IFS=,, still in Line 2 of the migrate script, sets the internal file separator to commas. If you absolutely absolutely need to have commas in your descriptions you could probably use IFS=$'\t' instead and export your spreadsheet as TSV.
